title: Hiring manager, senior software engineer, strong answers, tough

questions.text: Tell me about the largest cross-team system you led.
Tell me about a technical call where you went against the team's first instinct.
Why this role, and why leave the senior role you hold now?
How do you grow other engineers?
How do you handle an underperforming peer?
What would you do in your first 90 days?

persona.pushback_style: asks why not the simpler or the bigger option

brief.curveball: Midway through, say a key dependency team will miss its date by six weeks and ask how the candidate would re-plan.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi Joaquin, thanks for joining. I'm Marguerite, director of engineering for the platform group. We have forty five minutes, and I'll push on your answers a bit.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Hi Marguerite, thank you. That is fine with me.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: I saw you were at a conference last month. Was it useful?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Yes, one talk on event streaming was very good. I came back with a few ideas for my team.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: I'll ask about your largest projects and how you lead. I'll leave time at the end for your questions.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about the largest cross-team system you led.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: At Marrow Commerce I led the move of our order pipeline from a monolith to event streaming across four teams. I wrote the migration plan, chaired a weekly sync with the four tech leads, and took the on-call risk for the cutover. We moved in three phases over seven months with no customer-facing outage. Order latency at the 95th percentile dropped from 2.4 seconds to 600 milliseconds, and incident pages for that pipeline fell by about 70 percent.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What was the hardest disagreement between the four teams?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: The billing team wanted exactly-once delivery, which would have added about three months. I argued for at-least-once with idempotent consumers. I built a small prototype in a week and showed it handled replays with no duplicate charges in 10 thousand test events. Billing agreed, and I wrote the idempotency rules into a shared guide that two other teams reused.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a technical call where you went against the team's first instinct.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Our team wanted to rewrite the search service in a new language to fix slow queries. I profiled it first and found 80 percent of the time was one badly indexed query and a cache that never warmed. I proposed a two week fix instead of a six month rewrite. I owned the fix, and median query time fell from 900 to 210 milliseconds. I did note that the rewrite might still pay off if traffic triples.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why not do the rewrite anyway while you had the momentum?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Because a rewrite stops feature work for two quarters, and the team had committed to three launches. The fix gave us most of the benefit at about 5 percent of the cost. I also set an alert at twice the current traffic, so the question comes back with data, not opinion.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What did the team say when you changed the plan?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Two engineers were disappointed, since they wanted the rewrite. I gave one of them the profiling work as a lead task and let her present the results. That turned a loss into ownership, and she later led the cache redesign.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How do you grow other engineers?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I mentor three engineers at different levels. Last year I gave a mid-level engineer ownership of a service migration, and I reviewed her design docs weekly, not her code. I stepped back from the doc reviews after two months. She was promoted in the next cycle, and the migration finished two weeks early. For juniors, I pair on the first three tasks and then stop.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Say a dependency team just told you they will miss their date by six weeks. How do you re-plan?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: First I would find out what exactly is late and what we can build against a stub. Then I would split our plan into work that does not need it, which is usually 60 percent or more, and move that forward. I would tell product the new risk date today and offer two options, a smaller launch or a delay, with the cost of each. I would also offer the other team an engineer for a week if that gets them done sooner.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thank you. What questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: What is the biggest technical risk the team faces this year?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Our oldest data store runs near capacity. Moving it without downtime is the main risk, and we want a tech lead to own the plan.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That is all the time we have. Thanks Joaquin, we will be in touch within a week.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Marguerite. I enjoyed the conversation.

notes: Strong for senior: cross-team scope, numbers, trade-offs and mentoring. Handles pushback and the curveball.
